To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
inhalation of Ni3S2 by rats produces a dose-dependent inflammatory response in the lung and degeneration and/or atrophy of the nasal olfactory epithelulum.
the respiratory tract of F344 rats exposed to Ni3S2 for 3 months exhibits chronic active inflammation in lung and atrophy in the olfactory epithelia.

Ni3Sulfide is relatively soluble in the lung, inhalation of concentrations of Ni3Sulfid near the current Threshold limit value of 1 mg Nickel per cubic meter (Ni/m3) can produce detrimental changes to the respiratory tract after only a few day of exposure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
elucidating the mechanisms by which nickel compounds cause lung toxicity in experimental animals.
the effects of inhaled nickel compounds in rats.
the development and application of methods for assessing and quantifying the pulmonary toxicity of insoluble particles.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Ni3S3 is a pulmonary carcinogen in rats.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
inhalation of Ni3S2 produces a dose-dependent inflammatory response in lung that persists for several days after cessation of exposure.
Ni3S3, a highly insoluble form of nickel, is a potent pulmonary toxicant in the rat.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ni is a respiratory sensitizer and can produce significant lung toxicity at low concentrations.
the current Threshold Limit Values of 1 mg/m3 for nickel and its soluble compounds are too high and that a more stringent limit should be set for nickel subsulfide.
inhalation of 1 mg/m3 Ni3S2 for 3 months can cause chronic active inflammation in lung and atrophy in the olfactory epithelial layer in rats.
